title: Statistics, Data Displays, and Probability
lead: Part 2 of Problem-Solving and Data Analysis covers the statistics side: mean, median and range, data displays and standard deviation, probability from two-way tables, scatterplots and lines of fit, and the survey questions the SAT loves: margin of error, generalizability and study design. These questions look wordy, but they are among the most rule-based on the test.

parts.title: Part 1 · Mean, median, and range
parts.html:
Mean = sum divided by count. Median = the middle value when sorted, or the average of the two middle values for an even count. Range = maximum minus minimum.

The SAT's favourite questions ask what happens when the data changes.

ChangeMeanMedianRange
Add 5 to every value+5+5Same
Multiply every value by 3×3×3×3
Raise one value by 10, in a set of 20+10/20 = +0.5Depends on positionDepends on position

Changing one value changes the mean by (change) / n. The same logic answers “which value of x makes the mean equal K?”: the sum needed is K × n, then subtract the known sum.

Mean versus median. Outliers on the high end (a few huge salaries among modest ones) pull the mean up more than the median, so mean > median. The median resists outliers because it depends only on position. “Which measure best represents the typical value?” when an outlier exists → the median.

Common mistake. Forgetting to sort before taking the median. The median of 3, 1, 9, 4 is not the average of 1 and 9. Sort first: 1, 3, 4, 9, so the median is (3 + 4) / 2 = 3.5. The values arrive unsorted on purpose.

Frequency tables. When data comes as value × how many times, the mean is the sum of (value × count) divided by the total count. For the median, walk up the cumulative counts until you reach the halfway position. With 40 values the median sits between the 20th and 21st.

parts.title: Part 2 · Data displays and standard deviation
parts.html:
• Dot plots and histograms show the distribution: how many values fall at each point or in each interval. The most common value (the mode) is at the peak, where the dot stack or bar is highest. To find the median, count along to the middle position, as with a frequency table.
  • Box plots show the five-number summary: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum. The box runs from Q1 to Q3. Its length is the interquartile range (IQR = Q3 − Q1), which holds the middle 50% of the data. A box plot shows the median but not the mean.
  • Standard deviation measures how spread out the values are from the mean. Data clustered tightly near the mean has a low standard deviation. Data spread toward the extremes has a high one.

The SAT never asks you to calculate a standard deviation. It asks you to compare two data sets: the one whose values sit farther from its center has the larger standard deviation. Adding the same number to every value does not change it; multiplying every value does.

parts.title: Part 3 · Probability basics
parts.html:
Probability = number of outcomes you want ÷ number of outcomes possible. It is written as a fraction or a decimal between 0 and 1, where 1 means certain. Give it as a percent only when the question asks for a percent.

Example. A box holds 9 red tiles and 15 blue tiles. One tile is taken at random. What is the probability that it is red? Outcomes possible: 9+15=24
Outcomes wanted: 9
924=38

Start with the denominator. Before counting what you want, decide what group the choice is being made from. Most wrong choices on these questions have the right numerator over the wrong total, so settling the total first removes them.

A quick check. A probability can never be greater than 1, so the number on top is never larger than the number underneath. An answer such as 24/9 means the fraction is upside down.

The complement. The probability that something does not happen is 1 minus the probability that it does. When “not” covers many outcomes, this is faster than counting them.

The probability that a train arrives on time is 0.87. What is the probability that it does not arrive on time? 1−0.87=0.13

Probability from results. Some questions give the results of a trial or a count, with no list of equally likely outcomes. Use the results as given: times it happened ÷ number of trials.

A factory tests 250 light bulbs and finds that 15 are faulty. Based on these results, what is the probability that a bulb is faulty? 15250=0.06

Or, and, not. One small word decides the operation, so find it before calculating.

Words in the questionDo thisExample
or, eitherAdd, when the two outcomes cannot both happenA jar has 5 red, 7 green and 8 blue beads. Red or green: 5/20 + 7/20 = 12/20 = 3/5
and, both, thenMultiply, when one result does not affect the otherA spinner with 4 equal sections is spun twice. Blue and then blue: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16
not, exceptSubtract from 1Same jar, not blue: 1 − 8/20 = 12/20 = 3/5

parts.title: Part 4 · Probability from tables
parts.html:
Most SAT probability questions come with a table. A two-way table shows how two categories overlap: each row runs across and each column runs down. Fill in or check the Total row and column first, so you do not misread the table.

BusCarTotal
Grade 9302050
Grade 10254570
Total5565120

The probability that a student chosen at random takes the bus is 55/120, because the choice is made from all 120 students.

Conditional probability. The probability of A given B is (number of A and B) ÷ (total of B). The “given” condition shrinks the group you are choosing from, so the denominator is the total of one row or one column, not the grand total.

A Grade 9 student is chosen at random. What is the probability the student takes the bus? Given: Grade 9 → use the Grade 9 row only → 3050=35
A student who takes the bus is chosen at random. What is the probability the student is in Grade 9? Given: bus → use the Bus column only → 3055=611

How the wrong choices are built. For the second question, each wrong choice comes from one specific slip.

ChoiceWhere it comes from
30/120 = 1/4Right cell, but divided by the grand total
30/50 = 3/5Right cell, but divided by the Grade 9 total. This answers the first question.
25/55 = 5/11Right column, but the Grade 10 cell
30/55 = 6/11Correct: Grade 9 cell over the Bus total

Trap. The phrase that follows “a … who” or “of the … that” names the group. “A student who takes the bus is chosen” means the Bus column is the whole world for this question. The two questions above use the same cell and have different answers because the group is different.

More than one cell. If the wanted outcome covers two cells, add them for the numerator. “A student is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student is a Grade 9 student who takes the bus or a Grade 10 student who takes a car?” uses 30 + 45 over 120, which is 75/120 = 5/8. If a table does not name the category directly (“students who scored below 60”), count every cell that meets the condition.

Frequency tables. A frequency column shows how many items have each value. The total of that column is the denominator, and the frequencies of the values you want add up to the numerator.

A table with a variable. The hardest version puts expressions in the cells and gives the probability. Build the fraction the same way, set it equal to the given probability, and solve.

Example. One row of a table shows the number of red, green and blue marbles in a bag: 2x, x+3 and x−1. The probability that a marble chosen at random from the bag is red is 511. What is the value of x? Total: 2x+(x+3)+(x−1)=4x+2
2x4x+2=511
22x=20x+10 → x=5
Check: 10 red, 8 green, 4 blue → 1022=511

Where points are lost. The arithmetic is rarely the problem.

  • Calculating before working out which group the choice is made from.
  • Mixing up “or”, “and” and “not”.
  • Reading the wrong row or column, or missing a Total line.
  • Assuming equally likely outcomes when the question gives results to use.

parts.title: Part 5 · Scatterplots and lines of fit
parts.html:
Direction. Positive association (both rise together), negative (one rises as the other falls), or no association (a cloud).

Line of best fit, y = mx + b. The slope m is the predicted change in y per unit of x, in context: “each additional year of experience predicts an increase of $2,300 in salary.” The intercept b is the predicted y when x = 0. If x = 0 is outside the data, the right choice describes a prediction and does not claim it was observed.

Residuals. Residual = actual − predicted. A point above the line means the model underpredicted that case. If the line predicts 8.5 at x = 4 and the point is (4, 9.5), the residual is 1. “Which point has the largest residual?” means the point farthest from the line vertically.

Reading values. Interpolation (predicting inside the data range) is safe. Extrapolation (beyond it) is not. The least reliable prediction is the one farthest outside the plotted data.

parts.title: Part 6 · Margin of error, generalizability, and study design
parts.html:
These topics use almost no formulas, and each answers a different question.

Generalizability: can the findings extend to the whole population? This depends entirely on how the sample was chosen. A random sample of the population of interest generalizes. A non-random sample (volunteers, people at one location) does not, however large.

A researcher surveyed 5,000 visitors to the aquarium. Can the results be generalized to all city residents? No. Aquarium visitors are not a random sample of residents.

Sample size affects precision, not representativeness.

Margin of error gives a range for the true population value. If 58% of a random sample support a policy with a margin of error of ±4%, the true percentage is estimated to be between 54% and 62%. For “which value is plausible?”, check whether each candidate falls inside the interval.

Larger samples give smaller margins of error. If a question asks which change would decrease the margin of error, the answer is increasing the sample size.

Study design.

  • Observational study: researchers observe without interfering. It can show an association. It cannot show cause and effect.
  • Experiment: researchers use random assignment to a treatment group and a control group. Only an experiment with random assignment supports a claim of cause and effect.

Keep the two kinds of randomness apart. Random sampling decides who the results apply to. Random assignment decides whether you can say one thing caused another.

Tip. The questions have different triggers. “Can the results be generalized to all…” points to the sampling method. “Margin of error” or “likely between” points to the interval arithmetic. “Caused”, “leads to” or “results in” points to random assignment. Answering a generalization question with “the sample was too small” is the classic wrong move when the real issue is how the sample was picked.

parts.title: Part 7 · The Desmos angle
parts.html:
• Mean and median from a list: enter the data in a table and type mean(x_1) and median(x_1).
  • Missing value for a target mean: use the sum logic, or type (known sum + x) / n and the target as two expressions and read the intersection.
  • Line of best fit: enter the points in a table, type y_1~mx_1+b, then read m and b, or define f(x)=mx+b to evaluate predictions.
  • Probability: type the fraction from the two-way table, such as 30/55, to get the decimal when the choices are decimals or percents.

Statistics questions on the SAT are mostly reasoning, so Desmos is a helper here. The mean-change and interval logic should be done in your head.

parts.title: Part 8 · Combined groups, box plots, and predicted values
parts.html:
The mean of two groups combined is not the average of the two means unless the groups are the same size. Go back to the totals.

12 students have a mean score of 70 and 18 other students have a mean score of 80. What is the mean for all 30? Totals: 12×70=840 and 18×80=1440
840+144030=228030=76
The larger group pulls the mean toward its own value, so 76 is closer to 80 than to 70.

What a box plot does not show. A box plot gives the minimum, the quartiles, the median and the maximum. It does not show how many values there are, and it does not show the mean. Two box plots with the same span have the same range, whatever their boxes look like.

Predicted is not the same as observed. “Based on the line of best fit, what is the predicted value at x = 5?” is answered from the line at x = 5, even if a data point sits at x = 5 with a different value.

Estimating the equation of a line of fit. Read the y-intercept from the graph, pick two clear points on the line (not data points) for the slope, and eliminate: the sign of the slope and the sign of the intercept usually remove three choices between them.
